kcet|Chemistry|2015|30||0|0:
An essential amino acid is one the human body cannot synthesise, so it has to come from food.
There are ten: arginine, valine, histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine,
phenylalanine, threonine and tryptophan.
Isoleucine is on that list ✓
The other three are non-essential — the body makes them from intermediates it already has:
Tyrosine is made by hydroxylating phenylalanine.
Cysteine is made from methionine and serine.
Serine is made from 3-phosphoglycerate, an intermediate of glycolysis.
Note that tyrosine and cysteine are only non-essential so long as their precursors are supplied,
which is why they are sometimes called conditionally essential.
∴ isoleucine.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|31||0|0.s:
All four are sodium salts of an oxoacid of chlorine, so each is the salt of a strong base with
an acid of varying strength. The anion hydrolyses:
ClO⁻ + H₂O ⇌ HClO + OH⁻
The more hydrolysis, the more OH⁻ and the higher the pH. So the lowest pH belongs to the
anion that hydrolyses least — the conjugate base of the **strongest** acid.
Acid strength rises with the oxidation state of chlorine, because more oxygens pull electron
density away and stabilise the anion:
HClO (+1) < HClO₂ (+3) < HClO₃ (+5) < HClO₄ (+7)
HClO₄ is the strongest acid of the four — indeed one of the strongest known — so ClO₄⁻ is an
extremely weak base and barely hydrolyses at all.
Its solution is therefore closest to neutral, with the lowest pH of the set.
∴ NaClO₄.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|34||0|0.s:
The Hoffmann bromamide degradation converts an amide to a primary amine with one carbon fewer:
RCONH₂ + Br₂ + 4NaOH ⇒ RNH₂ + Na₂CO₃ + 2NaBr + 2H₂O
Look at the mechanism to see what it requires. The first step is removal of a proton **from the
amide nitrogen** by the alkali, and then bromination of that nitrogen. A second N–H is then
removed to form the isocyanate intermediate.
So the nitrogen must carry at least two hydrogens — the amide has to be unsubstituted, RCONH₂.
(1) CH₃CONH₂, (3) C₆H₅CONH₂ and (4) CH₃CH₂CONH₂ all have –CONH₂ ✓
(2) CH₃CONHCH₃ is an N-substituted amide. Its nitrogen holds only one hydrogen, so the
necessary second deprotonation is impossible and the reaction cannot proceed.
∴ CH₃CONHCH₃ will not undergo it.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|35||0|0.s:
Match the symptoms to the vitamin.
Cheilosis is the cracking and inflammation at the corners of the mouth, and it is the classic sign
of **riboflavin** (vitamin B₂) deficiency, usually with digestive disorders and a sore tongue.
The others each have their own deficiency disease:
Thiamine (B₁) — beri-beri, affecting the nerves and heart.
Ascorbic acid (C) — scurvy, with bleeding gums.
Pyridoxine (B₆) — convulsions and anaemia.
Riboflavin is found in milk, eggs, liver and green vegetables; it is water soluble, so it is not
stored and must be taken regularly.
∴ riboflavin.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|36||0|0.s:
Write the oxidation half reaction for water going to dioxygen:
2H₂O ⇒ O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻
Read the stoichiometry carefully: 4 electrons are released for every **2** moles of water, so
per mole of water it is 2 moles of electrons.
Charge = moles of electrons × Faraday constant
= 2 × 96500
= 193000 C
= 1.93 × 10⁵ C
The trap is option (2), 1.93 × 10⁴ C, which is simply a factor of ten out, and option (1), which
is the charge for one mole of electrons.
∴ 1.93 × 10⁵ C.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|37||0|0.s:
Esterification is second order overall, first order in the acid and first order in the alcohol:
rate = k[CH₃COOH][CH₃OH]
Now see what the dilution does. Each solution is diluted with an equal volume of water, so the
volume of each doubles and each concentration is halved.
[CH₃COOH] ⇒ ½[CH₃COOH]
[CH₃OH] ⇒ ½[CH₃OH]
New rate = k × (½[acid]) × (½[alcohol]) = ¼ × k[acid][alcohol]
rate(new)/rate(old) = ¼ = 0.25
The 1 M and 2 M figures never need to be used — only the *factor* by which each concentration
changes matters.
∴ 0.25 times.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|39||0|0.s:
Δ₀ is set mainly by the ligand, through the spectrochemical series:
I⁻ < Br⁻ < SCN⁻ < Cl⁻ < F⁻ < OH⁻ < H₂O < NH₃ < en < NO₂⁻ < CN⁻ < CO
Rank the four complexes by their ligand:
[Cr(CN)₆]³⁻ — CN⁻, a strong field π acceptor, large Δ₀
[Co(NH₃)₆]³⁺ — NH₃, moderately strong
[Cr(H₂O)₆]³⁺ — H₂O, weaker than ammonia
[CoCl₆]³⁻ — Cl⁻, near the weak end of the series, and a π donor, which pushes the t₂g level up
and narrows the gap further
Chloride is the weakest field ligand of the four, so it produces the smallest splitting.
(Charge also matters — a higher oxidation state increases Δ₀ — but all four metals here are +3,
so the ligand alone decides it.)
∴ [CoCl₆]³⁻.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|40||0|0.s:
Boiling point here is governed by van der Waals forces, which strengthen as the molecule gets
heavier and more polarisable. So order by molar mass.
iii. chloromethane CH₃Cl, M = 50.5, bp −24 °C
i.  bromomethane CH₃Br, M = 95, bp 4 °C
iv. dibromomethane CH₂Br₂, M = 174, bp 97 °C
ii. bromoform CHBr₃, M = 253, bp 149 °C
Bromine is both heavier and more polarisable than chlorine, so CH₃Br boils above CH₃Cl even
though the two are otherwise identical.
Adding each further bromine raises the mass sharply and with it the dispersion forces.
Increasing order: iii < i < iv < ii
∴ chloromethane < bromomethane < dibromomethane < bromoform.

kcet|Chemistry|2015|41||0|0:
The iodoform reaction needs either a methyl ketone, CH₃–CO–, or a secondary alcohol of the
form CH₃–CH(OH)–, which I₂/NaOH first oxidises to the methyl ketone.
Check each compound for that fragment.
(1) Propan-2-ol, CH₃CH(OH)CH₃ — has CH₃–CH(OH)–, oxidised to propanone ✓
(2) Butan-2-one, CH₃COCH₂CH₃ — a methyl ketone ✓
(4) Acetophenone, C₆H₅COCH₃ — a methyl ketone ✓
(3) Propan-1-ol, CH₃CH₂CH₂OH — a **primary** alcohol. The carbon bearing the OH holds two
hydrogens and no methyl group next to it in the required arrangement; oxidation gives
propanal and then propanoic acid, neither of which is a methyl ketone.
∴ iodoform cannot be prepared from propan-1-ol.
